s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz.title: Outgoing links are written, incoming links are built
s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz.reason:
A reverse link kept by hand survives the removal of its other end and then reads as a live relation. Rebuilt from scratch every time, the reverse direction is correct whatever was skipped before. Held in one list with the links the node makes, the links pointing at it show every relation of the node from where it stands. The end each entry names tells the direction.

A citation relies on the node it names as a link does. With no link of its own, a citation is seen only where it is written. Whoever changes the node it names then misses it. Quoted as code, as in a diagram drawn there, a citation relies on the node it names all the same.

A header's index and the values gathered beside a field copy what other nodes hold. The links stay with those nodes.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification. A link built to or from it would read as a live relation.

The SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab). A list in them of the links one project makes to them would hold true of that project alone.
doubts: Kept 'A node of the archive is held to neither: ...' as it stood: 'neither' may mean the two paragraphs above it or the two directions of a built link, and a rewrite would choose one.
s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz.split: Two requirements are carried out apart: a citation needs a declared link to the node it cites (written by the author), and the links pointing at a node are rebuilt and never written by hand (done by the tools).

s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm.title: A link carries its type
s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm.text:
Every link names what it means by one of these types:
- `implements` — the linking node is how the linked one is carried out.
- `refines` — the linking node states the linked node more precisely, or for a narrower case.
- `constrains` — the linking node holds a condition the linked rule depends on.
- `consumes` — the domain whose header holds the link uses what the linked section of another domain provides.
- `supersedes` — the linking node replaces the linked node, which is archived.
- `exempts` — a node of the project's own guidelines takes out of the rule that it is implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), for the reason its text gives, the linked rule or node of a project's own NodeKind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), or every such node under the linked section.
- `cites` — the linking node cites the linked one (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz), and no other type says how the two bear on each other. So it holds no link of another type to it.
- `term-relation` — the linking term and the linked term are bound, for as long as both exist, in the ratio the link carries.
- `uses` — what the linking term names makes use of what the linked term names while taking part in a process. For example, a user fills in a form while signing up. The link carries no ratio. A term that only starts a process, as an operator starting an export, uses nothing the process uses.

A `term-relation` link and a `uses` link bind two terms. No other type does, `cites` included: a term citing another term holds a `term-relation` or a `uses` link to it.

A ratio is the multiplicity of each end in the usual notation: 1, 0..1, 1..N or 0..N. The linking term's end comes first. For example, user 1:0..N session says that a user has any number of sessions and that a session belongs to exactly one user. Read from the linked term, the ratio is reversed.
s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm.reason:
A link without a type records only that somebody thought of two nodes together. No check can grade it. No diagram can draw it. A type named without its meaning is the same guess one step later.

Where no name of a type says more, a citation is typed by the words around it. So its link has a type of its own rather than none.

A use is kept apart from a `term-relation` because making use of something does not last and has no number to it. Given a ratio, a use states a multiplicity nobody means. A term that only starts a process takes no part in it, so a use of what the process uses would claim a part it never takes.

An exemption is a link rather than a mark on the exempted rule. So one node gives the reason for every rule it exempts, and each exempted rule outside the SpecSheriff guidelines shows, among its incoming links, what exempts it.

s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws.title: A link may cross a domain line
s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws.text:
A link between nodes of the specification may cross a domain line. A rule of one domain may point at a rule of another. Such a link carries its type like any other.

Whoever would point at a statement of another domain that no node there holds first gives the statement to a node of that domain. The link then points at that node, which is one of these:
- a node of that domain that can carry the statement;
- failing one, a rule written there whose `meta.todos` name the node linking to it.
s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws.reason:
Domains build on one another: a later one uses what an earlier one provides. The specification has to be able to say so.

A link holds the sid of the node it points at, so moving either node leaves the link whole. A link to a node that no longer exists is refused by the checker the same day.

A statement named in words rather than by a node is a reference no check can follow. The node it means then shows nobody relying on it.

Given to a node of its own domain, the statement keeps one home. A rule written for a link is read when its domain is. An item of its `meta.todos` says why it stands there.

s-hheus6f395ynqvc.title: The system's code is the code implementing the specification, and its tests
s-hheus6f395ynqvc.text:
The system's code is the code implementing the specification outside its guidelines, and the tests verifying that code. The implementing code includes code written by hand and code generated from the specification's nodes.

The repository's configuration, its own tools and the tests of those tools are not the system's code. A project's own checks and generators are among those tools (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze). The two are told apart by where each lives.
s-hheus6f395ynqvc.reason:
Code and its tests are written together, the test first (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). A rule counts as implemented only by a symbol carrying its SpecTag together with a passing test carrying its SpecTag (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf). So the tests belong with the code they verify.

Code generated from a node is part of the system as much as code written by hand. The repository's configuration and its own tools serve the work on the system, not what the system does. Where a file lives reads the same to every check, so it decides on which side the file is.

s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr.title: Code changes only as a consequence of the specification
s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr.text:
Behaviour changes by changing the specification first. The change to the code follows from it.

Every commit that changes code names, by its sid, each approved node whose implementation it adds or changes. This covers:
- a node whose text has just changed;
- an existing node the code contradicted.

Outside the tests, every SpecTag on a symbol the commit adds or changes names a node the commit's message names, or is the SpecTag that names none. The message names no domain's header and no section.
s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr.reason:
Wanting different behaviour is a reason to change the specification, not the code. A commit that repairs code which contradicted the specification as it stood is the same procedure and no exception to it. There the specification was already right.

The message and the SpecTags on the code name the same nodes so that the message says which nodes the commit serves. A header or a section is refused because it requires nothing a change could serve.
doubts: The original does not say whether the cases 'one whose text has just changed, or an existing one the code contradicted' are the only ones; the list is introduced by 'This covers' to leave that open.

s-rwqzepmrt77rv35.title: Three records, each answering a different question
s-rwqzepmrt77rv35.reason:
Each record answers a different question. The SpecTag on a symbol says what the symbol implements. The SpecTag a test declares says which rule the test is written from. Reported by a run of the tests, it makes the run itself a report of which rules are covered. The lists say what implements a rule, to a reader who has the rule open.

The SpecTag on a symbol and the one a test declares take one form, since each binds the code or the test to a node by its sid. A reference in that form is told apart from a sid that is only mentioned.
doubts: Kept 'three records' and 'All three' in the title and the text: they count the method's own records, not what a specification holds, so the rule on counts in prose seems not to reach them.

s-rah8b37kytb682y.title: The test comes before the code
s-rah8b37kytb682y.text:
When a rule is implemented, its test is written first. The code that implements the rule is written second, to pass that test. The test carries the rule's SpecTag (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35). So does the code that implements the rule (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4).

Every test carries the SpecTag of the rule, the term or the node of a project's own NodeKind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) it is written from. A test a commit adds or changes carries the SpecTag of an approved one.

A rule has at least one test where a commit adds or changes the code written for it. So does a node of a project's own NodeKind that needs code. Code generated from a node owes no test.

Rewriting a test's reference to its node into another form that names the same node changes no test.
s-rah8b37kytb682y.reason:
A test written first tests the rule, not whatever the code happened to do. A test names a rule's behaviour, which survives the refactoring that moves and renames the code underneath it. So the binding through tests is the stable one.

A term whose definition states behaviour is verified as a rule is. Its test carries the term's own SpecTag rather than that of a rule written only to repeat it. A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr).

Code generated from a node, as the types and RuntimeChecks of a RecordType are (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), is held by every commit to what the node produces (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j). So a test of its own would verify the generator rather than the system's code.

A test without the SpecTag of the node it is written from tests something nobody can name. A rule whose code has no test is carried out on trust. Both are refused where the change is made, which is when a test costs least to write.

A rule under revision is a draft while the tests written against its earlier wording still stand. So only a test a commit adds or changes must name an approved node.

A reference rewritten into another form names the same node, so the test is held to nothing new. Counted as a change, it would refuse, at the commit rewriting it, every test whose node is under revision.
doubts: Kept 'Counted as a change, it would refuse, at the commit rewriting it, every test whose node is under revision' as it stood: what 'refuses' is not named, and naming it would choose a reading.
The reason's first paragraph is reordered so that it opens with the ground of the main thought (a test written first tests the rule); no sentence's content changed.
s-rah8b37kytb682y.split: Three requirements are carried out apart: the test is written before the code; every test carries the SpecTag of the node it is written from, an approved one where a commit adds or changes it; code a commit adds or changes for a rule, or for a node of a project's own NodeKind that needs code, has at least one test.

s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4.title: Every symbol carries a SpecTag, and what carries no rule says so
s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4.reason:
A SpecTag on every symbol is what makes logic without a rule visible. A symbol left without a SpecTag until somebody changes it hides until then whether any rule asks for it. One SpecTag per file lets every symbol added to it later go untraced. A binding read by the domain a file stands in misses code that implements another domain's rule.

Code that serves the technology the system is built with exists because of how the system is built, not because of what it does. So there is no rule for it to cite. Demanding one teaches people to attach whichever sid is nearest. Marking it explicitly keeps 'nobody gave it a SpecTag' apart from 'there is nothing for a SpecTag to name'.

A rule under revision is a draft while the code written against its earlier wording still stands. So only a symbol whose code changes must name an approved node. A comment reworded, a citation moved or a name changed everywhere it is spelled changes nothing the code does.

A SpecTag counts as code because it decides which node the code is held to. Were a change to it not counted, a SpecTag could be moved onto a draft node, or onto one the code does not implement, with nothing refusing it.
doubts: Kept the first sentence with its enumeration '— a function, a class or a member of one, a type, a constant, a component —' as it stood: moving it into a sentence of its own would have to say whether it lists every sort of symbol or gives examples.

s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf.title: An approved rule is implemented or exempted
s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf.reason:
An approved rule states what holds of the system it specifies: what the system does or how it is built. So an approved rule the system's code does not carry out leaves the specification stating what does not hold of the system.

A SpecTag shows where the code carries the rule out (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4). A test naming the rule shows that the code does what the rule says, but only while the test passes. Every test of the system's code must pass at a push while the specification is approved (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh). Only both together show by a check that the code does what the rule says.

A SpecTag or a test of a rule implementing it counts, since an implementing rule is how the rule it implements is carried out (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm).

The SpecSheriff guidelines are carried out by the tools and the skills that apply them, never by code a SpecTag binds. A project does not hold that code. The repository writing the guidelines keeps it out of the system's code by where it lives (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc).

A project's own guidelines hold what only its specification needs (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab). They are carried out by those tools and skills and by people, not by the system's code. A rule of the technical debt describes a problem set aside, which is not required of the system and goes once it is solved (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

A rule the system's code cannot carry out, or that no test can verify, would be reported for as long as it stands. So such a rule is exempted. The exemption is a node, which one of its owners approves with its reason.
doubts: Kept 'a problem set aside, which is not required of the system and goes once it is solved' as it stood: 'which' and 'it' may stand for the problem or for the rule, and a split would choose one.
'only both together show it by a check' is written out as 'show by a check that the code carries the rule out'; please confirm that is what 'it' stood for.

s-zu8ne3wq84zchc4.title: The map is a mindmap of the specification
s-zu8ne3wq84zchc4.reason:
A specification is read one rule at a time and has to be understood as a whole. The two pull against each other. The full text is more than anyone holds at once. An extract loses where the rule sits.

A mindmap answers both: the shape of everything, and the detail of whatever is opened.

A diagram kept apart from the nodes is a second copy of the specification and disagrees with it silently. So the map is drawn from the nodes at each build rather than kept beside them.

The levels and the order of the domains carry how the domains bear on one another. Shown on the map, the statuses tell which parts of the specification wait for their owners while the whole stays in view.
